Definition: Percentage of individuals who used the internet (from any location, via any device) in the last three months. This measures actual internet adoption beyond network availability, capturing the combined effect of infrastructure, affordability, digital literacy, and relevance.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed, though the 72.9% figure in Comments is not what the cited source actually says. DataReportal Digital 2025 (GSMA Intelligence-sourced) reports 76.9% internet penetration (36.2m users) at start of 2025; Ecofin Agency cites ITU 2024 estimate of 77.4%. Both corroborate 70%+ (code 5); the exact percentage in Comments should be corrected to ~76-77%.

Definition: Unique mobile subscriber penetration rate as a percentage of the total population. Measures the proportion of individuals who subscribe to a mobile service (not SIM cards, which can be multiple per person). Mobile phones are the primary device for internet access in Africa.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed at aggregate level: ARPCE (Algeria's regulator, via APS/DzairTube) recorded 116.5% subscription penetration end-2023 (51.52m subscribers); ITU data (TheGlobalEconomy) shows 111.6 per 100 people in 2023; DataReportal shows 116-117% for 2025-26. All comfortably exceed the 70%+ threshold. Caveat: these are connection/subscription penetration figures, not strictly the "unique subscriber" measure the variable defines (which is typically lower due to multi-SIM use) — the last unique-subscriber figure found (GSMA, 2013) was only 48%. Code 5 is retained as directionally well-supported, but a current unique-subscriber percentage from GSMA Intelligence should be sourced to confirm precisely; flagged for human review on this definitional point.

Definition: The availability and presence of major cloud service providers (hyperscale and regional) operating in or serving the country with local or near-local infrastructure. Cloud availability determines access to scalable computing resources for government, business, and startups.
Value Name: Served remotely from distant regions only (>100ms latency)
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed no hyperscaler presence in Algeria: an independent academic study (Univ. of Cape Town, "Measuring Cloud Latency in Africa") confirms AWS/Azure/Google Cloud have no data centres in North Africa (only Cape Town, Johannesburg, Nairobi), and a secondary trade-press source corroborates no AWS/Azure/GCP facility in Algeria as of 2026, with Djezzy Cloud the only domestic IaaS option. Note the original citation (algeriatech.news) is an AI-generated content/blog site whose figures should be treated cautiously (see Tech Startup Ecosystem note below for a case where its figures conflicted with authoritative trackers); here its core factual claim is independently corroborated. Code 2 retained, source upgraded to the academic paper.

Definition: Whether the country has enacted legal or regulatory requirements mandating that certain categories of data (personal data, government data, financial data, or critical infrastructure data) be stored within national borders. Central to data sovereignty debates in Africa.
Value Name: Comprehensive requirements for personal data or broad categories
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed at code 4. Cookie-Script summary confirms Law 18-07 (2018, amended by Law 25-11 in July 2025) requires prior ANPDP authorisation for international data transfers and large-scale interconnections. A secondary (lower-confidence, blog-style) source describes additional layers — ARPT Decision No. 48/2017 requiring cloud/telecom data to be hosted locally, and a December 2025 Presidential Decree (25-320) mandating data residency for classified public-administration data — which would arguably support an upgrade to code 5 ("strict requirements covering multiple data types with enforcement"). Because this additional evidence rests on a single non-authoritative source, it has not been used to raise the score; flagged for human review to verify the decree specifics via an official gazette or UNCTAD/DLA Piper tracker before upgrading.

Definition: The presence and tier quality of commercial/colocation data center facilities operating in the country. Commercial data centers provide the physical infrastructure for hosting cloud services, content delivery, and enterprise applications domestically.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Original source (Cloudscene) was unreachable. Data Center Map lists several small commercial/colocation facilities in Algeria (Ayrade DC1/Tassili, Algiers Data Center, WebServices Data Center, ISSAL NET Oran, Syntys Algeria MDC Constantine) but none is confirmed as an independently-operated Tier III commercial colocation facility open to third parties. The only Tier III Design-certified facilities found (Sonatrach's internal datacentre and the government's Mohammadia national data centre) are private/state-enterprise and government facilities respectively, not commercial colocation providers. Code 2 (small-scale facilities only) retained as the best-supported reading.

Definition: Whether the government has established dedicated data center infrastructure and/or a government cloud (G-Cloud) strategy for hosting e-government services and public sector data domestically. Critical for data sovereignty and e-government service delivery.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Upgraded from 3 to 4. El Watan (independent Algerian daily) reports that President Tebboune formally inaugurated the "Centre national algérien des services numériques" at Mohammadia on 5 July 2026, built on two high-availability national data centres run in active-active architecture, connected to 46 government ministries and hosting the national public-services portal and national database. APS (state news agency, via aman-alliance.org) confirms the Mohammadia facility separately earned Uptime Institute Tier III Design certification in February 2026. This is a genuinely operational national data centre with an adopted national cloud/digital-transformation strategy (SNTN-2030), meeting code 4 ("National data center operational with cloud strategy adopted") rather than merely "basic".

Definition: Affordability of electricity for residential and small business consumers, measured as cost of electricity relative to income levels. High electricity costs are a direct barrier to ICT adoption and data center viability.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed with fresher data. GlobalPetrolPrices.com (Sept 2025) and Nairametrics (Q4 2025) both put Algerian residential electricity at approximately USD 0.041-0.043/kWh, among the cheapest in Africa owing to gas subsidies. At Algeria's GNI per capita (~USD 4,000-4,300), a modest monthly household consumption (~100kWh) equates to roughly 1% of monthly income, consistent with the "Affordable (1-2%)" band. Code 4 retained; original Eurostat source (2021, EU neighbourhood comparison) replaced with more current, country-specific pricing sources.

Definition: The maturity of the country's technology startup ecosystem, based on the number of tech startups, venture capital activity, accelerators/incubators, and the presence of a supportive ecosystem. Africa's startup scene is well-documented by trackers like Partech, Disrupt Africa, and Briter Bridges.
Value Name: Developing (growing startup base, regular funding rounds, several hubs)
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Cited source (Weetracker) is tangential — it covers a $1bn pan-African fund Algeria is contributing to, not the maturity of Algeria's own startup ecosystem. A widely-circulated claim that Algerian startups raised $650m in 2024 (algeriatech.news, an AI-generated content site) is NOT corroborated by authoritative trackers: Africa: The Big Deal put all of Northern Africa's 2024 funding at just $478m, with Egypt alone accounting for 84% of it, leaving well under $100m for Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and Libya combined — an order of magnitude below the $650m figure. Qualitatively, Algeria does have a genuine, growing base of hubs and government-backed early-stage funding (Algerian Startup Fund, Leancubator, Sylabs), consistent with "Developing" (code 3), so the code is retained, but the specific $650m figure in circulation should not be treated as reliable. Flagged for human review of the funding figure specifically.

Definition: The number and activity level of technology hubs, incubators, accelerators, and co-working spaces focused on technology and innovation. These provide physical infrastructure and support for tech entrepreneurship and skills development.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Upgraded from 2 to 3. Original CNN source was unreachable and, in any case, discussed AfriLabs' pan-African activity rather than an Algeria-specific hub count. AfriLabs' own directory lists at least four active member hubs in Algeria (Technopole Constantine Hill, PAUWES Entrepreneurship Hub, IncubeMe Algeria, Sylabs); an independent search additionally confirmed Leancubator, ranked Algeria's top incubator in a 2025 national ranking. Five identified, active hubs fits "3-9 hubs with regular activity" (code 3) rather than "1-2 hubs" (code 2).

Definition: The size and vibrancy of the local software developer and technology professional community. Measured through proxies such as GitHub activity, Stack Overflow representation, local tech meetup groups, and developer surveys. Indicates the country's capacity to build and maintain digital systems locally.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed with better sources. The original GitHub repo (32 stars) was too weak a proxy on its own. The 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey recorded 48 Algeria-based respondents (a visible but small share of ~35,000 total), and the independent "State of Software Engineering in Algeria 2024" survey drew 517 respondents, indicating an active, self-organising national developer community with local meetups (GDG Algiers, described as one of the most active GDG chapters in the MENA region) and an established computer-science training pipeline (see Tertiary ICT/STEM note). This is consistent with a "Developing" community in the low thousands rather than a mature, internationally visible one; code 3 retained, though an exact headcount could not be confirmed — recommend human review if a precise total is required.

Definition: The gap between men and women in mobile internet usage or internet access. Based on the GSMA Mobile Gender Gap data or ITU gender-disaggregated ICT statistics. A smaller gap indicates more equitable access to digital opportunities.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Directionally confirmed but evidence is dated. A World Bank survey document (2018 data) shows male internet use at 76.6% versus female at 60.6% — a ~21 percentage-point (relative ~21%) gap — which falls within "moderate gap (20-29%)". DataReportal's ~28% social-media-usage gender gap (2025) is broadly consistent but measures a different indicator (social media, not internet/mobile access generally) and no current GSMA Mobile Gender Gap or ITU gender-disaggregated internet-use figure specific to Algeria could be located (GSMA's Mobile Gender Gap report has limited North Africa coverage). Code 3 retained as the best-supported estimate, but flagged for human review: the underlying access data is up to 8 years old and a fresher, access-specific gender breakdown should be sourced if possible.

Definition: The scale and quality of tertiary-level ICT and STEM education programmes available in the country, based on the number and quality of institutions offering ICT degrees, computer science programmes, and engineering courses relative to the population.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Upgraded from 3 to 4 and re-sourced; the original citation was a World Bank "ICT in Education" country brief dated June 2007 — 19 years old and not usable as evidence of current provision. WIPO's GII country profile shows Algeria's science-and-engineering graduate share at 34.2% of tertiary graduates (ranked around 8th globally on that sub-indicator) with 52.6% gross tertiary enrolment. Algeria also has a long-established, selective national computer-science engineering school (École nationale Supérieure d'Informatique, founded 1969, ~180 engineering graduates/year, doctoral programme, two research laboratories) plus newer specialised institutions referenced in Algeria's own 2025 UNCTAD submission (National School of Artificial Intelligence, Sidi Abdellah Tech Park). This pattern of established, diverse institutions and a very high STEM graduate share supports "Good (established institutions with diverse ICT programmes)" (code 4) rather than "Moderate" (code 3). Also fills the missing Year with the corroborating GII/ESI evidence (2021-2025).
